speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. Yesterday the following telegram captioned "Urgent" was sent to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro):
In the matter of the dispute between Air Canada and Canadian Airline Employees' Association. CALEA recognizes Air Canada's legal rights under the Canada Labour Code. Nonetheless, CALEA finds Air Canada's action of June 16, 1976, inexcusable in light of the discrepancies of what the public is told and what the employees have been told. I hereby urge you to instigate an inquiry into the current dispute and also into Air Canada's labour relations policies and attitudes. We would be pleased to meet with you at your earliest convenience regarding this matter.
It is signed, J. T. Saunders, President, Canadian Airlines Employees' Association. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That the Minister of Labour, in view of the long-standing nature of the dispute and the unprecedented action of our national air carrier in locking out its employees, follow the very reasonable request by J. T. Saunders, President of the Canadian Airlines Employees' Association for an inquiry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister arising out of the cost-sharing proposals which the right hon. gentleman placed before the first ministers' conference. I should like to ask the Prime Minister if the government has done a costing analysis of the proposals giving the estimates of the financial impact on each of the prov-

inces and more particularly, as to whether or not the government has made any estimate as to what financial returns this would have given the provinces over the past years had these proposals been in effect and a projection as to what tax returns and revenues this would give the provinces over the next five years should these proposals go into effect.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FEDERAL PROVINCIAL RELATIONS
subsubtopic: ESTIMATE OF IMPACT ON REVENUES OF PROVINCES OF FEDERAL COST-SHARING PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I answered the other day I cannot give these estimates in detail. Perhaps some figures do exist in the Department of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and that of the Secretary of State, but as I emphasized to the House, and I think the premiers understand this well, the projection through the past of course would not be a fair indication of what we are doing. In the past we knew that these programs escalated at a very fast rate, something I believe in the area of 15 per cent or 17 per cent escalation per annum. We did not want this to continue and that is why we have resorted to capping some of these programs. But in the plan for the future we sought agreement from the House, the country and the provinces to limit the rate of escalation and instead of doing this through capping-

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVINCIAL RELATIONS
subsubtopic: ESTIMATE OF IMPACT ON REVENUES OF PROVINCES OF FEDERAL COST-SHARING PROPOSALS
speechtext: Capping?

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVINCIAL RELATIONS
subsubtopic: ESTIMATE OF IMPACT ON REVENUES OF PROVINCES OF FEDERAL COST-SHARING PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Yes, through capping, a difficult term to understand. I am sure the hon. member will be able to ask a supplementary. It would be a good day for him to do so. What we are proposing instead is a plan which would be composed of cash grants. These would be escalated more or less at the rate of growth of the national product. They would grow as the country grew. This is not possible to calculate in detail but every one would be able to plan on that basis. We know more or less the rate at which we hope to grow.
The other part would be in the form of tax points which we said would grow at least as fast or faster than the GNP. This is the problem with the fiscal dividend which would accrue from the fact that some of these tax points tend to grow faster than the rate of growth of the economy. So, it was a clear indication to the provinces of the principles on which this would be based which would permit them to make the calculations. I repeat that we may have made some estimates in departments but they are always conjectural. It depends upon the rate of growth of the economy.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROVINCIAL RELATIONS
subsubtopic: ESTIMATE OF IMPACT ON REVENUES OF PROVINCES OF FEDERAL COST-SHARING PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is obviously no absolutely direct correlation of which I know between the incidence of illness and the growth of the economy, but I take it the hon. member must recognize that the amount of money we can spend for health and education is not unlimited and that it is useful, if governments are to search out priorities and spend the public moneys in ways which meet those priorities, that they be able to do some planning. They cannot just say that they might have an epidemic next year and therefore they will have to let the growth escalate at an epidemic rate for the next ten years. There are obviously contingencies for which one has to plan. But the hon. member has been leader of a government which I think was notoriously successful in the management of its economic affairs, which never came near bankruptcy, so he must have been able to plan ahead what he would spend in various sectors of the economy including health, and I am sure he would understand this.

speechtext: In view of the fact that last year in the budget the former minister of finance announced that he was giving notice to the provinces of the termination of the five year agreement covering hospital insurance and diagnostic services, since this agreement still has four years to run, are we to understand that all the cost sharing proposals with respect to health services and post-secondary education are entirely contingent on the provinces accepting the immediate termination of the hospital insurance and diagnostic services, or is it intended that they will carry on for the four years which remain on the 50-50 basis and some other arrangement will be made about the other health insurance programs?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BASIS ON WHICH COST-SHARING FOR HEALTH AND EDUCATION WILL BE TERMINATED
speechtext: In the case of the post-secondary education the expiry date is April of next year, if my memory is correct. We talked about three areas at this conference. In the area of medicare, of course, the system of federal grants is already well established. The only case I think to which the hon. member's question refers would be hospital grants and we indicated that we were not going to accelerate the termination date of 1980. We were putting in place a program which hopefully would be able to bridge over the difference. If we can institute the program earlier, as indeed some provincial premiers suggested, we are prepared to do it sooner, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that in his statement to the conference. But it is not our desire to foreshorten this date if the provinces do not want to do so and we did not urge for it in any sense; we were merely responding to a suggestion by one of the premiers.

Mr. Speaker, it is fair to say that in my perception of it a great majority of the provinces favoured this scheme because it responded to a request the provinces have been making for a long time that there be a transfer of tax room and greater flexibility for the provinces in applying or in spending the money they receive from the federal government. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the sequence of events is not as the hon. member seems to suggest. The Minister of Transport indicated to me several months ago his desire to be in Europe at this time in order precisely to look into the kind of issue, amongst others, which is of concern to this country-safety in the air. Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to endorse what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Trudel) has said. I am pleased that we were able to arrive at a suitable amendment to clause 11 of this bill. As the House will recall, we raised this point extensively at second reading stage, pointing out that we felt the wording was most unfortunate and would, in effect, really have no practical application had it been left as then proposed. We pointed out that, while this is a relatively bulky act, it was an act that deserved the attention of hon. members since we were dealing with a very important aspect of our taxation system. So I am pleased that the amendment now before the House has been agreed upon.
There are two additional comments that I should like to make at this stage. First of all, I think it is most unfortunate that the government has represented to certain members in the private business community that the opposition has delayed passage of this bill. In no way have we delayed its passage. The history of it is that it was first debated in the House at second reading on April 2. It was reported out of committee, and I think both sides are in agreement that the changes made in committee are quite desirable. It was reported to the House on May 11. It has sat on the order paper, as far as this House is concerned, since May 11.
I would suggest we have debated a lot of things in this House without considering this bill, many of which could have been held in abeyance, giving higher priority to this measure. Certainly, we have indicated at all times that we did not intend to delay its passage if it were brought back for consideration. I am pleased that has been done today.
Income Tax
The third thing I would mention is the hope that before we complete third reading, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) will comment on the many points raised at second reading concerning the possibility of tax avoidance, or even fraud taking place to the extent of $1.6 billion involving Canadian companies. I am referring, of course, to the Globe and Mail report which was referred to at the second reading stage in April. At that time, the Minister of National Revenue said the figure was too high and made some rather casual comments.
It is important that before finally passing this bill, the Minister of National Revenue gives an explanation of what is being done in order to ensure that there is no tax avoidance or fraud taking place involving Canadian companies. Perhaps he could also indicate to what extent he thinks a problem now exists. I hope that in the time remaining someone will indicate, for hon. members present, the current position in respect of tax avoidance and fraud. subtopic: FINANCE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a few words about the bill before us. It should not pass in the kind of quiet oblivion which seems to have descended on the debate. While we are in favour of international agreements, generally speaking, the special position of Canada means that international agreements almost inevitably work to our disadvantage, especially in respect of taxation agreements. I say that in

June 18, 1976
Income Tax
this sense: most countries have a mutual interest in things, in the sense that there is a quid pro quo. However, given the higher level of foreign ownership in Canada, what happens is that almost invariably our treasury suffers from these agreements.
I know we take pride in being a good international citizen. I certainly take a personal pride in that, as I am sure do other hon. members of the House, and perhaps all Canadians. But increasingly I think that the kind of international agreement we are talking about should be given much more consideration than has been given in the past. We must temper our desire to be a good international citizen with concern about our national self-interest because of the high degree of foreign ownership and penetration into Canada by large, multinational corporations. This is not a national country in that sense, but a country which is more prone to paying more, because of this penetration, than any other. This applies not only to the matter of taxation and the repatriation of dividends, at whichever end they are taken, but it also applies to things like copyright and trade name laws.
Let us consider the situation in respect of patents, for instance. An international agreement in respect of patents is virtually worthless because we do not have, to any great extent, foreign patents. Relatively few patents are taken out in Canada, because if the multinational corporations who operate here make a discovery, they patent it in some other country. The same thing applies to trade or brand names. Brand names originate in other countries and, through our branch plant economy, these foreign names are used in Canada. This creates all kinds of problems when it comes to Canadianizing an industry, or the amalgamation by a Canadian company in order to take over and repatriate an industry to this country.
I do not think this bill should pass without this kind of danger signal being raised. It seems to me that in our great desire to go along with the rest of the world, we are creating these problems for ourselves. What I am really doing is kind of serving notice that from here on these international agreements, particularly when they concern ownership rights, repatriation of dividends and the kind of tax rates that can be levied, should receive much greater consideration then they have in the past. On many occasions in the past we have had to let things go because of lack of information. Let me point out one occasion on which I was very critical of the governor of the Bank of Canada who, at a time when Canada desperately needed to go on a floating exchange rate, because he wanted to maintain his friendship with other bankers around the world opted for a fixed exchange rate.
The point I made at that time, as others did, was that it is fine to be loved by all bankers around the world, and it is fine for everybody to pat you on the head when you meet with the bankers who say that little Canada, or big Canada, is a fine international citizen. But we are cutting our own throats. Many of these international agreements fall into that category.
I pose this dilemma, Mr. Speaker, but, quite frankly, I do not know how you reconcile the great feeling we have in this country, of being co-operative with the rest of the world and not being out of step, with what is going on in the world and is evidently working to our disadvantage

because of these international agreements. I think this is one of the great problems with which parliament will have to grapple.

It may be that as the afternoon goes forward, the parliamentary secretary or someone on the government side who may be knowledgeable in this field will enlighten myself and others in the House, particularly about my concern as to how the double-taxation system works.
Let us take, for example, the taxation system between Canada and South Africa. First of all, is there a doubletaxation system in this regard?

speechtext:
I raise this question because it is very relevant to the operations of Falconbridge in Namibia. I would like to know, if this kind of double-taxation agreement between Canada and Belgium follows this pattern, whether, in effect, this would be an improvement of any kind in respect of double-taxation with the third world countries where Canadian multinational corporations are exploiting their resources.
I hope the parliamentary secretary, or someone on the government side, will enlighten the House on this question, because if it means what we are doing is coming up with a nice dandy arrangement with the industrialized countries, I want to know how it might be improved to work for the benefit of the developing countries. I suppose it is very nice to have a double-taxation agreement which prevents individuals or companies from being taxed doubly in the home country as well as in the host country, but I wonder when the government will move on a policy to provide that Canadians are not double-taxed. That is an important question.
Canadians living in Canada are double-taxed. For example, in the lumber industry, if a person purchases lumber and the price of a sheet of oak veneer is $25, that price includes the federal sales tax and, on top of that, the 7 per cent provincial sales tax. There are other instances where
June 18, 1976

Canadians are double-taxed. I would be interested in seeing the government come up with a bill that would provide that Canadians not be doubled-taxed.
I am very happy to see that in this agreement taxpayers, at least, will not enjoy the tax haven which results from coming into Canada and teaching for two years without paying a penny of tax either in Canada or the country of origin. I am glad to see that this is not to be permitted. However, I wish some effort were made to review these conventions with other countries from which teachers come to this country and do not pay a penny of taxes for a year on the wages they receive in Canada. Those would be my concerns in respect of this bill. I trust that the parliamentary secretary or someone on that side will elucidate some of these points, because they are very important to me.

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AVOID DOUBLE TAXATION BETWEEN CANADA AND CERTAIN OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) should be congratulated for his attempt in this House to have a careful examination of this rather complicated piece of tax legislation. I wish to say a few words about some of the good things in the bill. I will deal first with the question of teachers.
For a long time we have had a convention with the United States under which teachers coming to Canada-I hope the parliamentary secretary will correct me if I am wrong-are given a tax exemption for two years. That is not a reciprocal tax convention; in other words, they do not have to pay the tax either in Canada or in the United States for a period of two years. I am not against international agreements with other countries, but it seems that we are being very generous with the teachers from foreign countries when we compare the treatment accorded our own teachers.
A great many of my constituents who work very hard in the lumber industry do not receive any exemption. They do not have access to the variety of deductions people have on the business side. I am pleased to see that in respect of France, Belgium and Israel we have ended this kind of situation. However, I would ask the parliamentary secretary-perhaps he has some information from which he can enlighten the House on this subject-to direct his attention to our situation in respect of other tax conventions, particularly with the United States, since many teachers come to Canada from that country, and with other countries in respect of which these tax conventions and tax concessions to teachers apparently still prevail. It is useful, of course, for someone wishing to settle in Canada to have a tax advantage, but it seems to me we are being far too generous with regard to the tax advantage given people from other countries. I am pleased to see that in these three cases we have started to move away from that particular concession.
I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe and the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) are to be congratulated for taking the stand that we should not pass these rather complicated bills without examination. Like the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, I do not argue that we should not enter into international conventions, but we have a very special problem in Canada because of the degree of foreign ownership and domination in this country by multinational, foreign corporations.
Income Tax
We know that Canada's multinational corporations, such as Falconbridge, operate on a world scale and perhaps avoid their fair share in contributing to the Canadian economy and the Canadian tax purse because of the lack of conventions or agreements with third world countries. It seems to me that in respect of a company like Falconbridge which goes into Namibia and employs workers there at a rate of something like 90 cents an hour, there should be a convention with that country to rationalize the tax position of Falconbridge. It seems to me we are in the position, surely, of having a moral duty to do all we can to prevent Canadian multinational companies from exploiting workers in the rest of the world.
One way in which we may be able to put pressure on the multinational companies to act in a decent and civilized way would be through tax conventions or agreements with third world countries. It seems to me that in respect of some of our tax convention legislation there is a wide area with which the government has not dealt, an area in which the churches of Canada are giving leadership. For instance, the United Church has taken an active role in respect of companies such as Falconbridge, in which it holds shares, in seeing that the international policy of such companies is consistent with Canadian standards in respect of their operations in the third world countries.
I welcome the legislation. We find it to be good. I do not have any heavy criticism of this bill. Mr. Speaker, there is somewhat greater latitude at this time to say a few things than there was on second reading. I want to make a general statement about the intent and purpose of the bill. I appreciate the parliamentary secretary's intervention and his reminder to the House that we are not talking about trade marks under this bill. I want to point out the essential difficulty with some of these international agreements, because if you wanted to find a subtitle for this bill it could be "How to make the world safe for multinational Corporations." I say that because the bill is not so much occupied with getting a fair share of the taxes from multinational corporations as with ensuring that they are not taxed in two places at the same time.
I appreciate that there is some element of fairness involved in this concept and we have to adhere to that element of fairness; but the consequence of a bill of this kind is really that multinational corporations can operate easily anywhere in the world. A bill of this kind facilitates the spread and the growth of multinational corporations around the world because, in effect, it provides international protection for them so they can move from one country to another and know what the ground rules are.
I am not going to diminish the importance of multinationals or anything else having a set of ground rules. I
June 18, 1976

think people should have ground rules; they should know where they stand if they are being asked to invest or if they are invited into a country in order to invest. However, what strikes me as being of far greater importance today than the signing of these kinds of agreements is that the world desperately needs an international convention regarding the behaviour of multinational corporations.
In a very lucid way, my colleague the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) pointed out the kinds of problems which are associated with the expansion of multinational corporations. Recently, at a Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in New Delhi, this was one of the central questions raised by all the Commonwealth members, because what is becoming quite obvious is that while many of the third world countries resent and find the yoke of the multinationals somewhat difficult, they are so desperate for development that they are willing to have development at almost any cost and under almost any conditions. Given the desperate straits of these countries and their needs, it is very easy for the transnational corporations-if we prefer to call them that, rather than multinational corporations-to strike outrageous bargains with one country, to its disadvantage in terms of taxation and its long-run benefits, as against another.
There are very few hon. members of this House who at one time or another have not been approached by people in large corporations-perhaps not directly, but in the course of conversation, debate, or on other matters-and told that, for instance, Ireland is giving the mining industry a 20-year tax holiday, or that some country in Africa is allowing 30 years without taxation, and that if Canada does not give the corporations that kind of deal they will not operate in Canada but will go elsewhere. I usually tell them to go elsewhere.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I do not lack confidence in this country to the extent that without the multinational corporations I think we are going to have to be crawling on our hands and knees, only to be told that we are going to go digging something out of the ground. I think we are quite capable of doing our own development, and we would have been much further ahead had we made that kind of decision. But the far greater problem with regard to multinationals is that there is a need to have some kind of international agreement which would prevent their playing one country off against another.
I realize that that kind of agreement cannot be too rigid, because some countries badly need investment and may have to pay a higher price and forgo revenue in order to get investment. That should be the free choice of those countries. But very often it is not a free choice, but a condition which is imposed because there is no UN, international body or international agreement which would limit the kind of arm-twisting tactics which are employed by the transnational corporations against countries which are really not strong enough to stand up for themselves. For that matter, a country like Canada, theoretically, should be strong enough to stand up for itself, yet somehow or other it gets its arm twisted pretty effectively.
That, to me, is the central problem. It is for that reason that, while in principle very few of us can be opposed to
Income Tax
international agreements, it strikes me as a bad set of priorities for us to rush into international agreements which are designed almost entirely to facilitate the work of transnational corporations and to make the world safe for them and their revenue, rather than-which in my view is a more important and urgent question-working out with other countries agreements for monitoring and for at least helping each other in terms of the kind of arm-twisting, and sometimes blackmail, which multinational corporations are able to inflict upon nations.
Therefore, as I said earlier, I do not see these agreements being of any great advantage to the average person in Canada. There might be a few pensioners who would benefit from this on a personal basis by not being subject to double-taxation in certain countries, but essentially it is not designed for that purpose. Whenever governments try to do something for large corporations, they always find a few widows, orphans and pensioners and throw them into the pot to show how even-handed they are and how the little man always benefits. But the point is that the problem of double-taxation in most cases does not affect those people. They do not make enough money in most cases to pay single-taxation, let alone double-taxation.
The problem is essentially that large and profitable corporations want to scoot around the world but do not want to get involved in the uncertainties of dealing with one country's tax legislation as opposed to that of another. If a corporation is a domiciled corporation in the sense that it has a physical presence in a country, it has to pay taxes on the same basis as any other corporation. But then all kinds of problems arise-and we know these problems arise- because profits are taxed. But how do we know what the profits are? The government, and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen), admitted that there are difficulties. The AIB, when we questioned it on how it was going to monitor profits, admitted that there are difficulties.
There is the transfer of royalties, which is a deduction against profits, and there is the payment of engineering fees, service fees and all kinds of other costs. In this bill, I see that those things have, at the most, a 15 per cent withholding tax on them and, at least, a 10 per cent withholding tax. That is a far greater problem, because trying to figure out what profit a transnational corporation is making in this country has been admitted by the Department of National Revenue itself to be impossible. For years the department has been trying-although I do not know how hard it has been trying-to monitor these things, but if pressed, and if it is in a particularly honest and frank frame of mind when it is pressed, it will admit that it does not have any control over these particular costs. Saying that the department is taxing the profits of multinational corporations the same as it is taxing any other company's profits is very misleading, because in very many cases the profits of multinational corporations are designed to be what they are prepared to demonstrate them as being to the Canadian government.
We see now that there is a tremendous outflow-probably a deficit of some $2 billion per year-of interest and dividend payments on foreign ownership in Canada, and we are now starting to see the bad effects. I think many of us have seen them for a long time, but more people are starting to see that the investment they made in Canada 10

The only thing that can be said about the agreement is that as a consequence of it we got the hon. member for Nickel Belt. There is always something good about legislation, whatever its defects.
I do not know how we ever got involved in this kind of agreement, and I do not know the thinking that went into it. It was typical of the era where some groups of people were picked out to be given favourable tax treatment and nobody seemed to think very badly of it. The argument was that if we did not give special tax treatment to offshore teachers coming to Canada, then our teachers would not get special tax treatment in the countries they go to. What is wrong with that? If Canadians go to another country, surely we expect them to contribute to the taxation of that country, whether they are there as guests or are working. We expect them to abide by the laws of the country and to be as good inhabitants as the permanent residents or citizens. I see no reason why Canadians should be given favourable treatment in other countries, or why people coming to this country should receive tax benefits.
Over the years I have received a great deal of correspondence from people working in our schools who complain bitterly about the tax load they carry in comparison to some of the people who came to Canada and who are virtually laughing at them. I guess it has been caused by the colonial mentality of some of the past governments of this country. I presume they were trying to entice people to Canada, as though we did not have enough teachers or university professors already.
If Canadians are going to countries that really are not in a position to provide their own teachers, I could understand if special financial arrangements have to be made in order to accomplish the national objectives of those countries. But why do it through the tax system? This is perhaps some of the justification for the teacher exemption in the third world countries; but most of the people who go there are not looking for special benefits, but go through a genuine desire to help. If they are to be compensated, it should be done in an above-board manner, either in the form of salary or a grant from one of the agencies involved in this country. The last thing we should do is alter the tax

system to handle a few specific problems. In that way the whole system gets fouled up and creates resentment amongst all kinds of people.
The government has acknowledged that the two-year period was not a good thing, and in the new agreements it is signing it is making sure that this benefit is not perpetuated. Most of us are trying to figure out how we got into this mess in the first place. Why did the government ever agree to this kind of measure? I certainly cannot recall the rationale for this move.
Mr. Speaker, while I welcome any move in the direction of international co-operation, and I think in many ways the new agreements we are signing are somewhat better than those we signed in the past, I want to record my concern about the ease with which we take these international agreements at face value. We have done little to explore them for the long run consequences to this country. In the case of the teachers, we probably thought it was a good idea at the time, but we have all lived to regret it.
While I am going to support this legislation because it has a number of good things in it, and my colleagues have indicated they intend to support it, I think there are many things in the bill we are passing today that we shall regret in the future. I think our optimism about international co-operation will be somewhat tinged with regret at making life too easy for the multinational corporations around the world under the umbrella of easy taxation.

I have not been able to get an answer to that question, but it seems to me that it is most important since so many U.S. teachers are coming to this country and are being given this tax advantage.
Another provision which is common to most other conventions, and from which the three countries mentioned in this bill are being exempted, is this: a teacher from a third world country who comes to Canada is provided with a two-year tax exemption. He has received his training in his country of origin in the third world. We are employing someone of great talent and skill who was trained to make a contribution in his own country. I am not against bringing such people to Canada, but I am against providing this kind of major tax concession.
I hope the parliamentary secretary can tell me what is the position vis-a-vis the United States. My understanding-I will be happy to be corrected if I am wrong-is that at the present time the United States is one of the coun-
June 18, 1976

tries with whom we do not have a tax convention. Surely, if ever there was a country with whom we do need a tax convention, it is the United States. I see the parliamentary secretary is shaking his head and I will not proceed if I am wrong, but my understanding is that a conscious decision was taken to allow the last convention to lapse, partly because of the introduction of the anti-inflation program of the government. If the parliamentary secretary is better informed than I am, I should be happy to hear what he has to say.
Another problem with international tax conventions continues to be the difficulty nations have in getting a fair share of tax revenue from multinational corporations. We face the same sort of problem in Canada in attempting to impose proper guidelines on multinational corporations. We do not have control of their internal bookkeeping, with the result that by overcharging for some services, and undercharging for others, they are able to escape tax. When a product is exchanged between a parent company and its subsidiary, there is no law that says it has to be exchanged at fair market value; therefore, revenue can be attracted by the company that will pay least tax.
There is, of course, a tremendous amount of manipulation going on in the world today on the part of multinationals in order to maximize their profits and deprive countries all over the world not merely Canada, of their fair share of tax revenue to which their citizens are entitled. I could give numerous examples of this sort of thing. The situation is similar to one of our boards that tries to regulate, for example, the investments of a telephone company. They may be allowed 6 per cent or 10 per cent on their investment, but what they are doing, in fact, is getting their own subsidiaries to sell them services well above market value, thereby siphoning off the profits into that subsidiary.
Take the case of a U.S. multinational corporation that has a Canadian subsidiary. The U.S. corporation can set rental rates for, for example, computer services. They can set the charges for a variety of other services rendered to the subsidiary, and as a result the profits of the Canadian subsidiary are reduced and thus fall within the AIB guidelines. This means that they can legally avoid the tax consequence. Then the parent company, whose head office may be in Bermuda or some tax haven like the Bahamas, gets all this money tax free.
Not only the Canadian public but people all over the world are getting a little tired of multinationals ripping people off. What we need desperately, and what I hope Canada will be party, to, is not merely bilateral tax conventions but an international tax convention that is administered by an international body like the United Nations, so that finally we can have equity and justice so far as the operations of these multinational corporations are concerned. At the moment they are operating well above the law and no nation has yet been successful in controlling the sort of manipulations that have taken place for such a long time.
The question of double taxation is interesting but quite often, instead of avoiding double taxation, as a result of the convention there is no taxation at all. Let me give the House an example of this. A British citizen who resides in Britain but whose revenues are obtained from Canada does
Income Tax
not have to pay Canadian tax on his Canadian income. He has to pay tax on his British income, but because he is a British resident his Canadian income is tax free according to the convention. This tax free money remains such, and Canada continues to lose this tax revenue. The British resident is able to obtain this tax free money because of an anomaly in the tax convention. That is not double taxation; that is no taxation at all.
There are many examples in this country where a loophole opens up as a direct result of that tax convention. When one looks at how aggressively this government has proceeded in terms of closing these tax loopholes, which admittedly it is attempting to do in the bill before us, it is interesting to go back through some of the clippings and attitudes of some of the ministers. For example, on June 13, 1975, in the Ottawa Citizen it was stated that the then consumer and corporate affairs minister, Mr. Basford, had pointed out that the government was about to strike out at those multinational loopholes. The article stated:
Revenue minister Ron Basford plans to spend more of the government's money in order to boost its revenues by eliminating tax loopholes.
The article then stated Mr. Basford said:
As society becomes more complex, as taxpayers become even more sophisticated, governments must invest more money in their tax systems to close the tax gap-
I have not seen any evidence in this House of that, but that was away back in June, 1975. There has been ample opportunity for moves in terms of the literally millions of dollars that Canada is losing. Let me give another example. I will quote from the February 24, 1976, edition of the Ottawa Citizen. The article is by Peter Cook and stated in part:
The federal government has shelved plans to close a tax loophole that costs the country "hundreds of millions of dollars" because the government cannot afford the expert investigators needed.
The loophole involves multinational firms that set up foreign subsidiaries and then divert income out of Canada to lessen tax liability.
Last June, Ron Basford, then revenue minister, said the practice was costing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost revenue. He promised a series of proposals to "significantly strengthen Canada's compliance effort."
The measures meant hiring experts to evaluate the cost of goods and materials being shipped in and out, and to set fair market values for tax assessment.
Revenue department spokesmen say government austerity measures have given the project low priority.
Surely we are being penny wise and pound foolish in this House when we start to cut things like expenditures on social services, yet we at the same time cut things in areas where we could increase tax revenues, such as the hiring of tax investigators and other people who could get out and try to stop the flow of legitimate tax funds from government coffers. We should be moving in these areas particularly in regard to the multinationals, so that they do not continue to milk the Canadian public as they have been doing for some time. The article continues:
The usual way of lessening tax payments is to underprice exports or overprice imports from a subsidiary located in a tax haven, or to charge artificially high expenses against the subsidiary.
To spot this, tax investigators must have thorough knowledge of the cost of materials and true market value.

June 18, 1976
Income Tax
Sometimes detection is impossible if a firm is shipping a new product, or if a product has a number of components. As an example, when oil is shipped to Canada from Venezuela via a tax haven, investigators may find themselves arguing over pricing of particular grades and chemical formulas.
Oil and chemical industries can best take advantage of this method of lessening tax. Very often, extra charges are laid against transportation.
The devices are there and they are being used, and it is costing Canadian taxpayers millions and millions of dollars every year. The poor fellow who works for wages in this country, who gets no deduction for anything appreciable at all and who sees the taxes taken off his cheque every month in advance, is getting a little tired of pious statements from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs about closing tax loopholes, while at the same time hearing statements that we cannot afford to hire extra investigators. I say this is something the government should be thoroughly ashamed of. It should be thoroughly ashamed of allowing the multinational corporations to siphon Canadian tax dollars without doing anything about it, without making the kind of investigation in depth, and without hiring the small research staff needed in terms of investigation so we can begin to attack the problem.
The bill before us does not attack the problem. It does not do anything at all about the problem. What we have done in this party is sort of give this a back-of-the-hand support. We should like to have seen some meaningful legislation which dealt with these tax and revenue transfers between the multinationals of one country and Canadian subsidiaries.
Another indication of the cost of this negligence can be found in this article by Mr. Jonathan Manthorpe in the Globe and Mail of October 31, 1975. This is what is said here:
Canada is losing hundreds of millions of dollars a year to people and companies that avoid taxes, and a lot of it is being lost to multinational corporations using their international status to shuffle their profits out of the taxman's reach.
James Gouriey, director-general of audit for Revenue Canada, says some of the multinationals use their intricate corporate structures to minimize the taxes they pay.
He said that at present there is not the staff, expertise or co-operation necessary among countries to stop them.
Mr. Gouriey said that for governments, "it's a very expensive type of tax collecting. Unfortunately we are up against the best tax brains in the world. These companies don't move today unless they know all the tax laws and then they just run around them all."
We need a combination of two things. We need to move toward international conventions in terms of the role of the multinational corporation in the world. But there is a lot we can do in Canada just in terms of turning our attention to the problem, such as hiring investigators and getting legal people to research and examine our own tax laws, at the same time looking at multinational corporations and the service charges between foreign companies and their subsidiaries. Surely we can move in this area to some extent, and then in the long range move to the international situation with world conventions in respect of this particular subject.
It is interesting to note that the government is able now to produce an international agreement between three countries and Canada which goes some distance toward rationalizing tax problems. However, our record in international agreements in another field, which involves the nuclear CANDU reactor, is a sorry one indeed in terms of

providing security to Canadians. We may be very much more secure in respect of companies and taxes as a result of this particular agreement, but we are doing nothing for Canadians in the field of providing international safey as we flog CANDU reactors like vacuum cleaners around the world.
Loss-leadering them.

We are loss-leadering them. We should be prosecuted under our own consumer protection laws for what we are doing with the CANDU reactor. That is an example of how not to go about entering international treaties. By moving very quickly in flogging this reactor we are doing a great deal to create the hazard of proliferation, for which this country may be ashamed in the future.
We will support the legislation. We understand the feelings of those countries that are interested, undoubtedly, in having the legislation passed. It is not our purpose to see this legislation unnecessarily delayed, but I must say that I resent any comment in this House that there is some kind of filibuster going on in respect of this bill. We are asking for the performance of a duty that every member of parliament should have, which calls for a careful examination of legislation that comes before them. That is what we are attempting to do in this party.
Is the House ready for the question?
Question.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

Agreed.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
No; this is just good sense. Mr. Speaker, I indicated in my remarks last night that someone had handed me a blank page and that I would try to carry on from there. I now have notes and I hope to be able to be a little more to the point this afternoon.
As we know by now, this legislation provides for capping federal contributions to medicare. The provision, of course, was for a 50-50 sharing formula. The legislation now provides that for the year 1976-77 there will be a cap of 13 per
June 18, 1976

cent, that in 1977-78 there will be a cap of 10.5 per cent, in 1978-79 there will be a cap of 8.5 per cent, and that thereafter there will be authority to set ceilings. That sounds innocuous enough, but really it amounts to the beginning of a complete change of philosophy and direction by the government.
I do not think the Canadian public is fully aware of the philosophic direction in which the government is moving. I am sure the government thinks it is moving in the direction the public desires in terms of social services. I think that at the next election members of the government will be very disappointed. The fact is that the country still needs a great deal in the area of health services. We have taken much for granted since medicare came in. Admittedly, this was a significant step forward, for which by the way full credit should be given to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who I believe should go down in history as the person who brought a decent, humane and proper approach to the provision of medical care. I hope history will give him the recognition he so richly deserves in respect of the policy for which he had fought over many years.
There are many areas into which we must move. One is the area of environmental health. An increasing number of people in this country are victims of cancer because of the way in which we treat the environment. When the federal government abandons its leadership role, and when it says, "We will leave it up to you fellows. We will give you some tax points, or you must use your own money", what it is doing is abandoning its role in providing quality medical care for Canadians.
There must be inducements for the provinces to move into new areas. By the abandonment of leadership in this field, at the federal level, we will be committing a great number of Canadians to ill health and even to death as a result of the failure to move in the field of research, the environment and preventive health care. We have completed the first phase of medicare in Canada. We have removed the financial burden which meant that a father sometimes would not send his children to a doctor because he did not have the money to pay the doctor. Much pride goes with poverty. There are examples, in the years before we had a medical care scheme, of people who literally were crippled as a result of the refusal of the family to seek charity, or simply because of their shame at not having sufficient funds.
Now, to the credit of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, and to the credit of people who came after him, such as Lester B. Pearson, that particular burden has to a large extent been lifted. However, we have not gone into the second phase, which must be a change in the delivery system relating to health care in Canada. That does not mean that we will eliminate private medicine, but we must have a two-stream medical system. In fact, we can provide a public health and public medical system and stream it alongside the private system. The two systems can be rationalized one with the other. In this way we can have public health services and public health doctors for treatment in those areas where we have difficulty establishing private medical clinics.
All through the north and in areas of my province there is need for a two-stream medical service delivery system. I
Medical Care Act
do not have anything against private medicine in particular; I think our doctors do a good job in Canada. However, there are many other areas of health where treatment is needed. There must be an expansion of medical services into the public area so that we can get to the real problem of health in respect of Canadians. I refer not merely to the treatment of sick people but to the question of keeping people well.
This lends itself more to the public health sector than to the private sector. There is an element of inefficiency in the private sector. Too often, if we go to a private clinic we see a large X-ray machine and other equipment and then see that equipment duplicated in the hospital down the street. It seems to me that the medical profession in the private sector could do a great deal to release some of the great amount of funds available to it.
One thing medicare has done is make sure that the doctors are reasonably well paid for their services. In the days before medicare, when some of us were young lawyers, a good percentage of the medical bills were never collected. Some doctors sent them to a collection agency, while others did not. A large percentage of the charges were not paid. That situation has been cured under the medical care scheme, and so it should be. The fact is the profession has been treated rather well by the medical care scheme.
I am pleased to note that the medical profession does not have a closed mind in respect of alternative methods of delivery. A great many of my friends in the profession talk about a two-stream system whereby we might place reasonable emphasis on the preventive area.
In respect of our medicare system, I believe we have a program which is superior to that in the United States. I do not say it is superior to that of countries in western Europe, because I think many countries are ahead of us. If we examine the percentage of the gross national product used for the provision of medical care in the United States, we find that it is 8 per cent. In Canada, even though we hear complaints about people going to doctors when it is not necessary, which I do not believe really is the case in many instances, the percentage of the gross national product is only 6 per cent for medical care. That is an indication that medicare is efficient.
The decision of the government to abandon medicare, in the sense of capping it, really flies in the face of the example which medical care schemes have provided. Canada's medical care scheme may be very closely copied in the next United States election as a platform for the Democratic party. We should be proud of what we have accomplished, although there is much more to be done. The government does not seem to be giving the Canadian people the leadership they want. The people do not want a fractionalization of the scheme. They do not want different standards for Prince Edward Island and Ontario. They want a national standard. They want to move into the area of prevention as a main lifestyle. Prevention means taking another look at the advertising of tobacco and alcohol.

When we look at prevention we must consider smoking, alcohol, and the provision of drugs, both medical and non-medical, which in my view are abused to a great extent. We must look to the government for leadership in lifestyle modification, changes in habits in terms of advertising and of trying to change public habits and attitudes in those areas which are so thoroughly unhealthy.
The next matter we should consider is nutrition. A dramatic example is the one of the farmers on Parliament Hill, which should make us realize that in a country which overproduces milk to the extent we do now, and where Coca-Cola is sold at approximately the same price, there is something wrong. We can make national provision of milk for school lunches right across the country without any trouble and at minimum cost. In the long run this will lower our medical costs because of the nutritional value of that product, which we should be pushing in our schools rather than pop and other junk foods.
We should encourage all Canadians to continue to have routine medical examinations. The result of this legislation will be the beginning of deterrent fees, a clear backward step from what we have become accustomed to. When we get back to the reasons for the bill, the argument is that costs are rising so fast and are so out of line that we have no choice but to cap them at this end. When you examine the figures, you find that sort of argument questionable indeed. The figures for the increase in medical care costs, the increase in the federal contribution, are quite interesting. When you break them down on a national basis, you find that in 1972-1973 the increase was 7.6 per cent; in 1973-1974 it was 8.8 per cent; and in 1974-1975 it was 6.6 per cent. Each year the increase was well below inflation in Canada, yet here we have a government which does not even want to keep its increasing contribution in step with the rate of inflation. Even that is too much. This is a niggardly, Scrooge approach to the question of the provision of medical care.
It is interesting that in my own province of British Columbia the federal contribution was 13.9 per cent in 1970-1971. It was reduced all the way down to 5.9 per cent in 1974-1975, and 1974-1975 was the year of the NDP government in that province which allegedly was squandering money; at least this was the theory abroad. It is certainly not indicated in the provision of medical care in that province or the reduction of the federal government's contribution to those medical services. As I say, the capping is unnecessary. The costs are not increasing at a rate which is inordinate or unreasonable, and by limiting the increase we are taking away the provincial inducement to move into new areas.
One area with which I want to deal now and which I think is most important is environmental health. More and more in this country we find that as we alter the natural state of the environment, as we provide new chemicals and new pesticides, and as we provide insulating materials such as asbestos and new plastics, new forms of cancer emerge. We cannot let that happen to the Canadian people. But by abandoning the federal contribution in medicare

that is exactly what we are doing. The standard of living that we have in this country in the south is now becoming dependent upon the poisoning of Indians in the north.
It is to our shame that we see at English river, in northwestern Quebec, in Mistassini and other places, our native people suffering from Minamatas disease. The reason they have been suffering from Minamata disease is that the standard of life in the south is higher. We have industrialized areas in the north and we have taken risks with the future of the Indians. What are we repaying them with? The most we are doing at English River is to tell them not to eat the fish.
It is time we did something in terms of full compensation for native people but, most important, it is time we learned a lesson from Minamata disease in this country, that you do not move into an area in a rush for spoils, profit and money in the process of which you destroy the environment and kill the native people. That has been the tradition in this country. Let us make no mistake about it. We have nothing to be proud of in the way we settled Canada, in terms of our native population. That is what we are still doing when we consider the mercury poisoning that is now taking place in these areas of Canada.
We have a real problem with vinyl chlorides in the provision of plastics. Liver cancers are developing at an alarming rate. The interesting thing about preventing cancer is that it takes 20 years for lung cancer to develop in asbestos workers. The workers themselves do not feel the immediate risk, although they are running a high risk daily. They need the money, they have to continue to work. We cannot sit idly by as parliamentarians, nor can this government sit idly by and let this continue. We still do not have mandatory regulations regarding the use of masks in asbestos mines. Admittedly, we brought in some ambient air standards.
We still have not done anything with regard to tailings or with regard to drill standards. The wind can blow tailings all over the place. Only a minor amount of asbestos causes cancer. Are we to abandon the fight against cancer because of this government's niggardly approach to medical care and its tragic departure from principles in which they once believed? There is no question that what we are seeing in Bill C-68 is the end of the purported just society and the end of those great promises of 1968. It is all over now.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the amendment put forward by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) is a very wise one indeed. What we see happening with respect to the acUons of the government with regard to medicare reminds me of the definitions of a Tory and a Liberal. A Conservative is one who stands at the seashore, sees someone drowning 20 yards offshore, throws out a rope which is 15 yards long, and expects the drowning person to show initiative and swim the other five yards to catch the rope. A Liberal is one who stands at the seashore, sees someone drowning 20 yards offshore, throws out a 20 yard rope, and when the drowning person grabs the rope and starts pulling, the Liberal drops it. That is the kind of thing we see in Bill C-68. The government is trying to beat a hasty retreat from a program which has proved to be what the government expected it to be.

speechtext:
I do not know. There are some Tories who would do other things with the rope.
The medicare program in Canada has been held up by the government as an exemplary program. The United States sent representatives from its Senate, led by Senator Ted Kennedy, to come here and study our medicare program, the universality of our program, and the way the program is operated, because the Americans do not have a similar program. This government was very proud to run around beating its breast and holding up its program as being exemplary.
However, what do we find the government attempting to do in Bill C-68? The government has proposed a withdrawal from an area which is vital to the national health and security of this nation. Indeed it is rather interesting to note the unilateral action which is being proposed by the government. Here we have a government which has talked about co-operative federalism and said that the decisions in Canada are made through discussions between the federal government and the provincial governments, and that they try to work out co-operatively decisions which are acceptable to all sides. Bill C-68 jettisons that whole concept of co-operative federalism, and the government is taking a unilateral position with respect to medicare.
When we entered into medicare, it should be noted that it was the socialists of Canada who pushed and pushed for a minimum level of medicare and of health services in this country and finally obtained it. After having been promised it since 1919, we finally ended up with a medicare program.
The present program was held out by the federal government, and the federal government encouraged the provinces to join and participate in providing medical care coverage. It might not affect wealthy provinces so much
Medical Care Act
when the federal government withdraws from some of the areas of medicare coverage, but it seems to me that the poorer provinces in Canada will have a very difficult time reaching even that minimum level of medicare and health services to which their citizens have become accustomed. It seems to me that it is only right that the whole question should be reviewed after six months, instead of moving with such undue haste into this area. This is what we are saying in the amendment of the hon. member for New Westminster.
This motion would give the government the opportunity to go back and sit down with the provincial ministers of health to try to work out an agreement which would ensure that the medicare services of this country are maintained. Indeed, they should not only be kept at their present level but should be expanded to cover many of the other areas which the hon. member for New Westminster pointed out in his excellent presentation this afternoon.
We on this side of the House have said time and time again that any tampering with the present medicare act will result in a loss of services to parts of the country which cannot afford to pick up the cost of carrying the program. There can be no doubt that this bill may damage forever both the quality of health care in Canada and the quality of our health insurance program.
Canada's health system has served the people of this country very well, and it is only right that at this point in time this party should vehemently protest any changes which will cause a reduction in the delivery of health care services across the country. When our party first introduced this idea in Saskatchewan, it fought the vested interests. There is no question that there were some who were opposed to medicare. This party fought for the right of every man, woman, and child in that province and in the country to have the benefits of decent health care. This party fought for an idea which would guarantee access to the needs of life, and it also fought so that we would not have to depend on wealth alone to provide what is essential and what is a right of Canadians.
Where were the Liberals and Tories at that time? We knew where they were. They opposed that idea. They used all kinds of excuses. They called it socialism and interfering in the lives of the Canadian people. Then they used the old bogeyman of cost and said that we could not afford a universal medicare program. We have experienced that kind of opposition over the years, and that is why we are so leery about Bill C-68. We see it as the thin end of the wedge to revert back to the situation where only those who have wealth will be able to enjoy health care. That is what we are leery about, and that is why we take such a firm stand in opposing any changes of this kind in a unilateral way.
We know that the Liberals in Saskatchewan fought medicare tooth and nail. It was only because of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and his colleagues that the Liberals of Saskatchewan were dragged kicking and screaming into the twentieth century. Looking back at the scene in Canada, that seems to have happened federally as well. The federal government did not like medicare but gradually we forced them to accept it

June 18, 1976
Medical Care Act
because it worked so well elsewhere. They are all running around now boasting what a fine medicare program we have, yet they are ready to use the scalpel on it. The Liberals had never liked the program. I would be the last member in this House to accuse them of being politically motivated, but they finally picked up the idea and saw it had some relevance and acceptance in the country.
Were the Tories any different, Mr. Speaker? Look at them in Ontario today. Frank Miller runs around the province like some avenger, just turning up at a hospital and telling the administrative staff that it is being closed down. We saw that with Doctors' Hospital in Toronto, but the staff there won a stay of closure in the courts. Now the Ontario government has appealed that. The Doctors' Hospital was serving the ethnic people in one area, and indeed some of the staff speak many languages. This is the kind of action which can only discriminate against newcomers to this country who might not be familiar with our ways. The Tory government in Ontario talks about restraint, but not about restraining itself. Why does it not start restraining its own expenditures instead of hacking away at essential services?
The federal Tories are not any different. The Canadian Medical Association tells us of the need for psychiatric care, but here in the Ottawa area they are cutting down on psychiatric beds, and this after we have been told they are one of the biggest needs in society today.
The Tories and Liberals have never supported programs like medicare but have always opposed them. It was only because of the vision of people like the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and members of his party and of the CCF who fought for and achieved their goals that we have this program today. Now the government wants to hack away at it, but we are not going to stand here and let it take it apart piece by piece in this phony fight against inflation. It is all right to fight inflation, Mr. Speaker, but the government blew $16 million bucks and we have not got even one plane for it. Members of the government should be ashamed of themselves. They go out and elect one guy who has an ego as big as the Olympic project, and build the Olympic project for $1.5 billion without batting an eyelash.
Today we talked about the multinational corporations getting away without paying over $1 billion that is due in taxes. The government talks about fighting inflation but what kind of fighters are its members? It has often been referred to as "the law of the sea" kind of thing-it is women, old folks, and the unemployed first, but the corporate citizen sits back at the Rideau Club with his Liberal and Tory friends and gets the benefits of the fight against inflation. That is shameful. Then they have the gall to say they are interested in people.
The government says we are spending too much on medicare and on the health of the nation, but as has been pointed out previously the percentage of our Gross National Product spent on health care has been dropping, not increasing. One thing we cannot afford in this country is to have people debilitated by lack of proper medical care. We hear a lot about the man days lost through strikes and lockouts. The Tories are famous for asking questions in the House about this, but do we hear about the number of man days lost due to sickness? The number is triple that of the

time loss due to labour problems, and it is growing. Why do we not tackle that type of problem?
We know something about industrial diseases in my area. Surely the government could do something through Atomic Energy of Canada or the commissions and acts that exist. It is the government's responsibility to ensure that people working in the uranium mines are not exposed to undue danger. Would it not be cheaper to prevent a person contracting silicosis that to treat him afterwards? This government and the Ontario government have reneged on their responsibility to see that safety levels are enforced. We read of the asbestos workers at Kananaskis walking around with asbestos fibres in their feet and breathing the fibres that float around the atmosphere. We have to ask what price we are going to have to pay 25 years from now perhaps to support their widows and orphaned children. We are now faced with the cost of the carelessness of those people who had responsibility for enforcing health standards at the INCO and Syncrude plants.
The cost of preventive medicine and delivery of services to those parts of the country that do not have them surely cannot be considered in the same light as the health of the people. Surely there is no comparison, Mr. Speaker. There are certain things that Canadians have a right to such as decent housing at reasonable cost, and education for the people as far as their abilities will take them. And we have said, although this government has never accepted it, that every Canadian has the right to a job. There ought to be a policy of full employment. Surely the other right that Canadians have is the right to adequate health care whether they live in the outposts of Newfoundland, in Vancouver, Toronto or Nickel Belt. Surely Canadians who live in the slow growth areas of Canada have as much right to the best medical services available as Canadians living in downtown Toronto who may earn $40,000 per year.
Surely all of our people have a right to decent medical care. My party believes that the government, by introducing Bill C-68, has retreated from that concept. For that it should hang its head in shame. Its action is despicable. It is limiting the rights of the people of this country to proper health care.
Those are not the only rights the governments has eroded. The right to free collective bargaining, for which many people were jailed, for which others were knocked on the head, and even died, went through the window when the government introduced the anti-inflation program. At present the right of our people to decent health care and medicare is being attacked and eroded by the government. We shall oppose that process of erosion as far as we can. We have proposed an amendment which we hope is accepted.
The government ought to consider again, with the provincial ministers of health, the status of the present program. That, it seems to me, is only fair. We should not cut back with regard to medicare. Instead, we should consider expanding the program. When the government talks about saving money by cutting back on health care, it does not take into account what these cutbacks will cost the people. Those costs one cannot calculate.
June 18, 1976

We ought to be concerned about the nutrition of our children. Having taught for 16 years in the province of Ontario I am aware of what some children eat and know how well nourished or otherwise some of our school children are.

speechtext: The whole gang of them are doing it. You will see when we become the government in Ontario what we shall do to this province's educational system. It will be the envy of the world. I have seen the results of the Nutrition Canada survey commissioned by the government. I do not think government members read reports which the government itself has commissioned. speechtext: The hon. member looks pretty sleek.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA

speechtext:
The hon. member is purring. Government members should be encouraged to read government commission reports. If they did, perhaps they might be more inclined to spend money where it ought to be spent, instead of cutting back on essential services.
Government members ought to be encouraged to read the Treasury Board's report about injuries in the Public Service of Canada in 1974-75. According to that report, in the year 1974-75 there were 22,218 accidents in the public
Medical Care Act
service which cost us, directly, over $7 million. Over 10,000 of these injuries took place in that department which considers itself the friend of the working class, the Post Office. Almost 7,000 of those injuries were disabling. As I said, the total cost of public service injuries was over $7 million. That cost does not include the cost of medicare given to the people involved. I suggest that the true cost of the injuries would be much higher if one included the cost of medical care.
In Ottawa, I discovered that the majority of lung-related diseases are caused by smoking. In the riding of Nickel Belt, lung-related diseases, in the main, are to be found among people who live too close to the smoke stacks of Inco and Falconbridge. Whenever it seems that corporate profits may dip, the first item of equipment to be sacrificed is anti-pollution equipment-thanks in large part to the attitude of federal and provincial departments concerned with the environment.
I have spoken of ways to improve the quality of life with preventive medicine. We are lagging in that field. It seems to me that preventive medicine can lead to cuts in medicare cost. We should be thinking in terms of such cost cuts, instead of in terms of such arbitrary cost cutbacks as the federal government is now proposing, cost cutbacks which will lead to a lowering of the already minimal level of the country's health and medical care services.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA

speechtext: What about home care nursing?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA

speechtext: I agree with the hon. member. At present we have chronic care patients occupying active care beds which cost us at least $100 per day.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: That's an example of government waste.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA

speechtext:
That is right. We need more efficiency in the field.
In Ontario, because of the Tory government's approach to hospital costs, many nurses will be out of work. I understand that some 3,000 nurses have already been laid off in Ontario. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) blames the nursing schools and universities for not projecting properly the job market. But how could the universities know that the federal government was to cut back its participation in medicare?
The minister has blamed the universities, whereas the fault lies with the government which created the difficulty in the first place. It is like blaming the rape victim for her own predicament. That is despicable. Why did the minister not tell the universities beforehand that the government intended to cut back with regard to medicare? Why did not the Tory government in Ontario take the universities and post-secondary institutions into its confidence and tell them what it wanted to do? The nurses are available. Surely we need not keep chronic care patients in active care beds at over $100 per day.
We have heard little about rehabilitative programs. Surely it would cost less per diem to apply rehabilitative measures than to keep certain chronic care people in active care beds, at great cost.
The government has not even considered the paramedical field. Many people in remote parts of ridings must
travel over 100 miles in order to get emergency attention.

June 18, 1976

Surely such attention could be provided by paramedical workers. Little has been done in this regard.
The government can do all sorts of fine sounding things. It can bounce a signal off a satelite to provide television and communication coverage for corporations and frontier regions.

That looks like a make-work project, and it seems to me that these things all cost money. Some of these projects cost a heck of a lot of money. But we are not afraid to do this.
The Bank of Canada is erecting a building across the road made of glass. When it was started it was to cost a modest $30 million. The figure has now jumped to $75 million. They have some exotic plants in there now, the like of which I have not seen since I left Latin America. I go over there, Mr. Speaker, when I want to feel at home. Yes, Mr. Speaker, it will cost $75 million, and they don't bat an eyelash.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA

speechtext: They have been building like that since the Spanish conquistadores.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA
