speechtext:
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cam-bridge is right. Ever since the conquistadores came to this country.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) got up in this House and said we are to have a national lottery to raise money until 1989 and then we shall be able to pay off the Olympic debt-if it costs every widow the last ten dollars she ever had. We are prepared to go to those lengths for the kind of monuments Shelley referred to, the kinds of monuments that will stand in the desert and just crumble apart in the sands of time.
When it comes to those services which affect the quality of life for people, surely the government has to say: those things we will not touch-there are certain agreements we will not back away from. On the contrary, we should be expanding those particular kinds of agreement in the areas we have mentioned before.
I remember the time when I taught in the schools. We had no money to pay for speech therapists. Children with speech disabilities received no special attention: their problems were ignored in the hope they would go away. School boards and taxpayers could not afford to support speech therapists in the school system. The same was true of children who were hard of hearing. We were not prepared to let a private member's bill go through this House-the Tories were dragging their feet on it, I know- which would set the upper limits of noise levels in any one place to 85 decibels. They were not prepared to let that

through. I thought it seemed to me to be a very fine bill, one which we could do with in the work places in the Sudbury area; the vast majority of those who work for the mining companies are suffering from some kind of hearing disability.
There is something which will always be held against the government sitting over there. It is the fact that it was not prepared to move in an aggressive way in the area of preventive medicine. Surely, we on this side of the House ought not to be the ones to stand up and press the government to retreat from its position-a position which we consider to be a totally backward step with respect to the provision of medical services.
I have talked about some of the documents which were commissioned by the government. I want to read from the Ontario Economic Council report a rather interesting section on health issues and alternatives, published in 1976. This is what is contained in this particular document:
The situation with respect to industrial health and safety may be worse than it seems because many industrial health problems remain undetected or unreported and in the Council's view we lack professionals specializing in industrial medicine. We have too few investigators and inspectors. There are several thousand toxic chemicals used in industrial processes but standards have been set for only a few hundred.
If the government wants to spend money, if it wants to avoid wasting medicare support, the best way to save is to spend money in these particular areas of industrial health safety and preventive kinds of health problems that are presently put upon society. If, beyond that, the government wants to save money, it can do it.
One of the comments made by the hon. member for New Westminster was that we should start taking a look at home care so that we can assure that active care beds in hospitals are occupied by active care patients. It seems to me this step would be a good one for patients, not only because they could be taken care of in their home environment enjoying the love and comfort of their family, but also because it would mean saving money for the taxpayers of Canada.
As I mentioned before, there are many parts of my own riding where we have to depend on emergency services which may be a hundred miles away. The people who live and work in those areas do not get a cut on their OHIP premium-they just pay the same OHIP premiums as I pay, living in a town where medical services are close and readily available. The effect of this bill will be to create even more difficulty for these people.
We talk about dental problems. The government has no dentacare program at all. It has been left completely up to the private sector; it has been left to workers in a particular situation getting into a collective agreement. But the minute they get a dentacare program established, what happens? The dentists put their fees up overnight to grab the highest possible charge they can. The government has reneged in this matter. It is fairly obvious that those who are in an organized shop can get the benefit of a dentacare program. But, once again, those workers who are not organized, usually lower-aid workers who do not have the strength of collective agreements, are left without the benefit of a dentacare program for themselves and their families. The government has not moved in the area of expanding medical services to include a dentacare program
June 18, 1976

which would be of preventative benefit. Instead, it is quite prepared to sit back and cut away existing programs.
I have said that the Liberal government which sits over there is not unlike the Tories-we have seen an example in Ontario. One of the costs which drove up medicare in Ontario was the rip-off which took place by the private labs. There we saw the doctors and the private labs working hand in glove and ripping off the taxpayers.

speechtext: No, not all of them, but certainly more than 2 per cent of them. Studies in Ontario and elsewhere in this country have shown that approximately 2 per cent rip off any social welfare program. Interestingly enough, in Ontario the rip off of the OHIP program among doctors was 10 per cent-five times as great, Mr. Speaker. So when the hon. member on the government side of the House talks about percentages he should keep things in proper perspective. We have seen this kind of rip off by the private labs in Ontario, and it has added to the cost of medicare. Some hon. members give the impression that only the working class and people on welfare rip off the system. Rip-offs are not confined to poor people, the rich people rip off the system more so.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to prolong this debate; I just want to make a couple of points. The New Democratic Party in particular has tried to portray this bill as being a cutback in expenditures on hospitalization and medicare. In fact it is no such thing. It simply sets out the growth rate at which the federal government will continue to participate in the medicare scheme. The NDP persist in talking about cutbacks in hospitalization. This bill has nothing whatsoever to do with hospitalization.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) made a few valid points and it is too bad he wrapped them up in so much red rhetoric. I can understand why it is he would want to increase expenditures on medicine; it is because he is suffering from a bad case of verbal diarrhea this afternoon. The fact that must be on the record is that this bill has nothing to do with hospitalization. It deals only with the limit to which the federal government will go in increasing expenditures on medicare.

Mr. Speaker, I had not planned to speak at all on this bill, but after the nonsense I have heard from the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) I feel I must say a few words. However, we do not think the government should do this unilaterally without first negotiating with the provinces.
The NDP are in a great position to tell us what they would do. If anyone recalls what they did to the province of British Columbia within the short space of three years, they drove the province into half a billion dollars worth of debt.
